clue.text: Coats not necessarily made of green stuff

definitions.text: Coats not necessarily made of green stuff

parts.words: Coats not necessarily made of green stuff
parts.note: the first part of these coats' name is a green vegetable, so the clue wonders whether they are sewn from it

explanation.surface: A remark that certain coats need not be made of green cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: A pea is green, so the name sounds as if the coat might be made of peas; it is in fact a short heavy woollen coat worn by sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: These are short double-breasted woollen overcoats traditionally worn by seamen.

clue.text: Cast one's vote for such an all-rounder ?

definitions.meaning: to ... for a candidate is to vote for them alone
read literally, someone round all over, that is chubby

explanation.surface: Choosing a versatile cricketer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all-rounder' suggests a versatile sportsman, but here it means someone rounded all over. An all-rounder in cricket is a player who both bats and bowls.
explanation.definitionFit: To plump for is to choose firmly; as an adjective it means pleasantly fat and rounded.

clue.text: Materials for building those imaginary castles ?

definitions.text: Materials for building those imaginary castles

parts.words: Materials for building those imaginary castles
parts.note: imaginary castles are castles in the air, so their bricks would be made of air

explanation.surface: Daydreamers' building supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: Castles in the air are daydreams; the answer is really a perforated brick that lets air through a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A perforated brick used for ventilation, whose name suggests bricks made of air.

clue.text: A bit of a fight, the whole fight too — so things get rumoured

parts.note: a round is one section of a boxing match
and means in addition, like too
a bout is a complete contest, as in a boxing bout

explanation.surface: A boxing commentary that spills over into gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: A ROUND is part of a boxing match, A BOUT the whole of it; rumours spread far and wide in every direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumours that spread in every direction travel all over, here and there.

clue.text: "—don't last: cookery do!" (Meredith)

parts.note: a line from George Meredith's novel The Ordeal of Richard Feverel, with the first word left blank to fill in

explanation.surface: A quotation from a Victorian novelist saying good cooking outlasts romance.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line from Meredith's The Ordeal of Richard Feverel sets romance against cooking: the affection fades, the cooking stays.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Meredith's line is the romantic act set against cookery.

clue.text: Neaera's locks in need of attention

definitions.text: Neaera's locks in need of attention

parts.words: Neaera's locks in need of attention
parts.note: recalls Milton's Lycidas, 'the ... of Neaera's hair', and hair that needs combing

explanation.surface: A woman's hair badly in need of a comb.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's Lycidas speaks of sporting 'with the tangles of Neaera's hair'; uncombed hair is full of knots. The held text adds 'my', which the page does not print.
explanation.definitionFit: Knotted, matted strands of hair are what Milton's line gives Neaera, and they need combing.

clue.text: She gets two numbers of the Arabian Nights !

indicators.note: two of these numbers asks for the same letters written twice in a row

parts.note: the Arabian Nights are the Thousand and One Nights, and 1001 in Roman numerals is MI

explanation.surface: A woman receives a pair of stories from the Arabian Nights.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'numbers' are not tales but figures: the collection is called the Thousand and One Nights, and 1001 is MI in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: Mimi is a woman's name, best known as the heroine of Puccini's opera La Bohème.

clue.text: It seems to be not uninhabited in the main

definitions.text: It seems to be not uninhabited in the main

parts.words: It seems to be not uninhabited in the main
parts.note: split the word into a verb and a past participle meaning rented out, so occupied by tenants; the main is the sea

explanation.surface: A remark about a place being mostly occupied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the main' seems to mean mostly, but the main is the open sea. Read as IS LET the answer says it is rented out, hence not uninhabited, though a little sea island usually is.
explanation.definitionFit: A small island in the sea, whose spelling also reads as a statement that it is rented.

clue.text: In rude surroundings five are unable to pay their way

indicators.note: rude surroundings means the word for rude goes round the other piece

parts.note: insolent means rude or disrespectful
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: Five people in a shabby neighbourhood who cannot make ends meet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surroundings' puts INSOLENT (rude) around V (five).
explanation.definitionFit: A person or business that cannot meet its debts is bankrupt.

clue.text: Puffed with exercise and such a noisy bore!

parts.note: pneumatic means filled or worked with air, puffed up
drill is military exercise

explanation.surface: Someone out of breath from a workout who is also a loud tiresome talker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bore' looks like a tedious person; it is a tool that bores holes, worked by compressed air and very loud.
explanation.definitionFit: An air-powered road-breaking tool that bores into the ground with great noise.

clue.text: Eradicates our post in a reshuffle

indicators.note: a reshuffle rearranges posts, so the letters of the preceding words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A cabinet reshuffle wipes out one of our government posts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a reshuffle' rearranges OUR and POST.
explanation.definitionFit: To pull something out by the roots is to destroy it completely, a synonym of eradicate.

clue.text: Puzzle no more French ?

parts.note: non is French for no
plus is the French for more

explanation.surface: A puzzled question whether the French language has had its day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' governs both words: NON PLUS is French for 'no more', and it is also an English verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To nonplus someone is to bewilder or perplex them, so it is a synonym of the verb puzzle.

clue.text: Long lasting belly noise, but without an inner turn

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside, so the bell's sound is wrapped round the other piece

parts.note: read as bell-y noise: the noise of a bell, a peal

indicators.note: turn tells us to write the word inner backwards

explanation.surface: A rumbling stomach that goes on and on, though the gut never churns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'belly noise' is a pun: bell-y noise, the sound a bell makes. 'turn' reverses the word inner, and 'without', in its old sense of outside, wraps the bell's sound round that.
explanation.definitionFit: A perennial thing endures year after year, so it is long-lived or enduring.

clue.text: Some account I like to live up to

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An account of someone that the speaker wants to measure up to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes part of 'accoUNT I Like'.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer means up to a certain time, as in staying on to live up to that point.

clue.text: Hadji's place

parts.note: a hadji is a Muslim who has made the pilgrimage, so his place is the city of that pilgrimage

explanation.surface: Where a pilgrim lives or belongs.
explanation.walkthrough: A hadji (hajji) is a Muslim who has made the hajj, the pilgrimage to the holy city in Saudi Arabia.
explanation.definitionFit: The holy city in Saudi Arabia is the goal of the hajj pilgrimage, so it is the pilgrim's place.

clue.text: For the dispatch of postal tuition courses ?

definitions.text: For the dispatch of postal tuition courses

parts.words: For the dispatch of postal tuition courses
parts.note: post is mail and tuition is coaching, so a vehicle carrying correspondence courses

explanation.surface: A service for sending out correspondence courses.
explanation.walkthrough: Post is mail and tuition is coaching; the answer is the old horse-drawn coach that carried the mail.
explanation.definitionFit: A stagecoach that carried letters and passengers along fixed routes.

clue.text: Light cloak ?

parts.note: read not as a thin garment but as the mesh covering a gas flame that glows to give light

explanation.surface: A thin cape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' looks like an adjective meaning not heavy; it is the noun, the lamp, and the 'cloak' (mantle) is the glowing mesh hood over a gas flame.
explanation.definitionFit: This mesh hood fits over a gas jet and glows white when heated, giving light; mantle also means cloak.

clue.text: Beauty was the theme of Robert Bridges's

definitions.text: Beauty was the theme of Robert Bridges's

parts.words: Beauty was the theme of Robert Bridges's
parts.note: the poet laureate Robert Bridges wrote a long philosophical poem titled The ___ of Beauty

explanation.surface: A remark on what a poet laureate wrote about.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Bridges, Poet Laureate, published The Testament of Beauty in 1929.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in the title of Bridges's 1929 long poem, which means a will or declaration of belief.

clue.text: I'd one suit to be turned

definitions.text: I'd one suit to be turned

indicators.note: a garment that is turned is worn the other way about, which signals rearranging the letters before

explanation.surface: Someone who wants a suit turned so the worn side is hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be turned' rearranges I'D, ONE and SUIT; a suit that is turned is worn with its lining outward.
explanation.definitionFit: A turned garment has its lining on the outside, the reverse of the normal way.

clue.text: "Ask where's the North? at York 'tis on the Tweed: in Scotland at the (Pope)

definitions.text: "Ask where's the North? at York 'tis on the Tweed: in Scotland at the (Pope)

parts.words: "Ask where's the North? at York 'tis on the Tweed: in Scotland at the (Pope)
parts.note: lines from Pope's Essay on Man, whose next word is the Latin name for the Orkney islands

explanation.surface: A quotation from Pope about how the north keeps moving further away.
explanation.walkthrough: In Pope's Essay on Man, each place thinks the true North lies further on: York says the Tweed, Scotland names the Orkneys by their Latin name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin name for the Orkney Islands, the next word in Pope's line.

clue.text: Cratchit Minimus, Peter and I take a lot of beating

parts.note: Tiny Tim is the youngest Cratchit in Dickens's A Christmas Carol; minimus is old school slang for the youngest of brothers
Peter Pan, J M Barrie's boy who never grew up

explanation.surface: Three characters who are hard to beat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take a lot of beating' usually means are excellent; here it is literal, as kettledrums are beaten. Minimus is the English public-school tag for the youngest of brothers at a school.
explanation.definitionFit: Kettledrums in an orchestra are struck with sticks again and again.

clue.text: How those special supplements are presented

definitions.text: How those special supplements are presented

parts.words: How those special supplements are presented
parts.note: extra pages are put in among the others, or a small extra picture is set within a larger one

explanation.surface: A question about how magazine supplements are delivered.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra leaf or small panel placed inside a larger publication or map is called this.

clue.text: Small comfort for the peckish

parts.note: the phrase small comfort is taken literally: a tiny morsel for someone a little hungry

explanation.surface: Something that does little to console a hungry person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small comfort' is an idiom for little consolation, but here it is a tiny piece of bread; also a bird pecks at it.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny fragment of bread or cake would barely satisfy someone who is slightly hungry.

clue.text: If money talks, so do forgers

definitions.text: If money talks, so do forgers

parts.words: If money talks, so do forgers
parts.note: forgers pass false money into circulation, and the legal word for that is the same as the word for speak

explanation.surface: A cynical saying about counterfeiters and the power of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: To utter forged money is to put it into circulation, the legal term; it also means to speak.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means both to speak and, in law, to pass counterfeit coins or notes.

clue.text: Those engaged in dramatic errors?

parts.note: points to Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors and to actors in such plays

explanation.surface: Actors who fluff their lines on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dramatic errors' recalls Shakespeare's The Comedy of Errors; those working in comedy are funny performers.
explanation.definitionFit: Performers in comic drama, as in Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors, are the people meant.

clue.text: Places for viewers, say ?

indicators.note: say tells us the word that follows is spoken, giving the sound of the answer

parts.note: sights are things for viewers to look at

explanation.surface: Spots chosen for spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Places for viewers' looks like one phrase; 'Places' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Locations or plots of ground are synonyms of places.

clue.text: A maze with no gap

parts.note: close the space between the two words and they make a verb meaning to stun with surprise

explanation.surface: A labyrinth with no way through.
explanation.walkthrough: A maze with no exit sounds plausible, but the 'gap' is the space between A and MAZE: closed up, they give amaze.
explanation.definitionFit: Amaze and the answer are synonyms, both meaning to overwhelm with surprise.

clue.text: Fruit ingested by a worker for instance ?

definitions.text: Fruit ingested by a worker for instance

indicators.note: something ingested is swallowed, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a worker is a classic example of an ant, the worker ant
a lime is a citrus fruit

explanation.surface: A piece of fruit eaten by a labourer as an example of food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ingested by' means swallowed, so the fruit goes inside the worker; read whole, the clue says fruit eaten by a worker ant is an example of its food.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for food or nourishment, which fruit eaten by an ant would be.

clue.text: Swift runner sounds musical

indicators.note: sounds says the word for the musical is pronounced like the answer

parts.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical

explanation.surface: A fast athlete with a good singing voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'musical' looks like an adjective; it is the noun, the show Hair.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-eared animal is famous for its speed over open ground.

clue.text: So a cellist plays swing

indicators.note: the letters are made to play about and take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A cellist performing swing music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plays' rearranges SO, A and CELLIST.
explanation.definitionFit: To move back and forth like a pendulum is to sway regularly.
